# Answer key — Chapter 13: The integrated case {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-13-csf-mapping · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
@sec-13-csf-mapping names the six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect,
Detect, Respond and Recover. Option a mixes in incident-response phases,
option c course layers, option d the CIA triad and GRC terms.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-13-csf-mapping · basic)* — **Correct: a.**
The chapter says Govern is drawn at the centre because it sets the strategy
and policy on which the other five depend; it is Respond and Recover (not
Govern) that stand ready for the incident.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-13-hardened-stack · basic)* — **Correct: c.**
"These layers are independent by design, and that is what makes them one
system rather than a list": the firewall catches what the WAF would not, MFA
catches the stolen password, monitoring catches what all of them let
through — defence in depth as structure. Option b states the opposite of
independence.

**Q4** *(tests @sec-13-csf-mapping · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"defensible does not mean the service cannot be attacked; it means the
protection is complete across the framework at the level of Categories, and
for each Category the control, the threat it meets and the reason it
belongs can be named" (any phrasing with both halves: not
attack-proof; completeness across Categories with a nameable
control–threat–reason for each).

**Q5** *(tests @sec-13-argument · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"because a cloud-native application is a complex distributed system and the
system keeps changing, the position must be argued again as it changes",
"security lives inside complexity; only a position argued anew as the
system changes, never a permanent yes" (any phrasing that ties the answer
to the complexity of distributed systems and/or to the system changing, so
the argument must be remade).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-13-csf-mapping · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The chapter: "An empty Category is a real gap, because a service with no
entry under Detect is blind and one with nothing under Recover cannot come
back." Option c inverts the closing exercise's point that a thin Function
is a gap in the defence rather than in the exercise.

**Q7 — applied scenario** *(tests @sec-13-closing-exercise · applied)* —
**Model answer:** The argument fails the chapter's test of completeness:
defensible means every Function (and Category) is populated, not that one
Function is strong — the Functions are independent layers, and each catches
what the others miss. Concretely, nothing under Govern means the
organisation cannot answer for its security (no risk register,
no shared-responsibility mapping, no regulatory frame), and nothing under
Recover means the service cannot come back after an incident. Populating
Govern: the risk register / shared-responsibility model / NIS2-DORA-ISO
22301 frame (S12) — threat: unmanaged, unaccepted risk and unmet
obligations; risk: the organisation cannot prioritise or answer to
regulators; control: the register aligning mitigation with risk appetite.
Populating Recover: tested backup restoration and disaster recovery /
business continuity (S11, S12) — threat: data loss or destruction that
prevention did not stop; risk: permanent loss of the service and its data;
control: off-site, tested backups and a rehearsed recovery plan. Grading
notes: full credit needs (i) the completeness-at-Category-level rebuttal,
(ii) the concrete meaning of each empty Function (answer for it / come
back), and (iii) one course control per Function stated as
threat–risk–control; partial credit for correct controls without the
vocabulary.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

The source chapter provides no sketch answers: its only exercise is the
open-ended closing exercise (@sec-13-closing-exercise), which is assessed
against the group's own hardened service. The standard it sets is the one
quoted in the chapter: at least one entry per Function, each defensible in
the threat–risk–control vocabulary of Chapter 1, with thin Functions or
Categories treated as gaps in the defence to be found now.
